lead: When you can't figure out how to do something well, ask instead: how could I be sure to mess it up?
when: When you're preparing an event, handing in an assignment, planning a trip, or have a plan that sounds great but you keep worrying you've missed something, try checking it in reverse first.
body:
When we're about to do something, we usually ask, "How can I make this succeed?" But that question is so broad that all we come up with is "try harder" or "be more careful." Flip it around and ask, "What would make this hard to pull off?" and the answers tend to be much more concrete: preparing at the last minute, not checking the requirements, putting it off until the end.

Inversion is a way of thinking that analyzes a problem from the direction opposite to the goal: first identify the conditions that would block the goal or cause failure, then look for actions that reduce or eliminate them. It complements forward planning and helps uncover obstacles that are easy to overlook.

Write down those pitfalls, then work out how to avoid each one, and you'll have a preparation checklist you can actually follow. For example, "don't be late" becomes "check the route ahead of time and leave an extra twenty minutes for transfers."

"Inversion" here means checking the same goal from the other direction. It isn't about contradicting everyone, and turning a sentence backwards doesn't make it wise. You still want things to go well. You're just looking for holes by starting from the ways in to failure.

Thinking backwards isn't just reversing the order of the steps. You can start from an outcome you don't want and trace back to its causes, then turn each cause into a preventive action. The causes may sit side by side; they don't have to be forced into one chain where each inevitably leads to the next.
example:
You're organizing a get-together with friends this weekend and want everyone to have a good time, but you don't know where to start. First ask, "What would make the trip a waste of everyone's time?" Ideas come easily: sending the wrong address, finding no seats when you arrive, forgetting to ask who can't eat spicy food, and people having no way to get home afterward.

So you send the location in advance, book a table, ask about dietary needs, and check when the last train leaves. These steps may not make the gathering spectacular, but they rule out a few letdowns that could easily have been avoided. With those handled, you can plan games and little surprises with more peace of mind.
extra: If you want to use your phone less, first ask, "What would keep me scrolling forever?" All notifications turned on, the phone right by your pillow, and opening short videos every time you're bored. So you might turn off unnecessary notifications, put your phone across the room before bed, and keep a book handy for bored moments. Then keep watching for whether you've just found a new way to procrastinate.
steps: Write down one specific goal, such as "submit a proposal that meets the requirements by Friday."
Flip it and list the three things most likely to make it fail, focusing on ones you can influence.
Turn each one into a preventive action, then check afterward: what else is needed to actually reach the goal?
caution: Avoiding the conditions for failure isn't the same as meeting the conditions for success. Showing up on time doesn't mean you'll pass the interview, and complete paperwork doesn't mean the proposal is any good. And don't let this turn into endless worrying: deal with the two or three most realistic risks, then move forward.
exercise: Pick a small task you need to finish this week and complete the sentence: "If I wanted this to fail, I would..." Write three answers, then choose one and take a preventive step right away.
brief: The reverse structure of inversion planning: on the right, the goal is a reachable flagpole; on the left, a stick figure is setting out. A gray line along the top works backward from the goal through failure points such as a stumbling stone, a broken bridge, and a leaky boat, with the stick figure marking obstacles from back to front and repairing the bridge. Along the bottom, a navy route runs from the start to the goal, avoiding the obstacles that have been identified.
